topic.title: Rational Functions and Holes
topic.summary: When the graph of a rational function has a hole instead of a vertical asymptote, and how a limit locates the hole.

lesson.title: Rational Functions and Holes
lesson.summary: When the graph of a rational function has a hole instead of a vertical asymptote, and how a limit locates the hole.
learningGoals: 1.10.A Determine holes in graphs of rational functions.
lesson.bigIdea: A rational function can be undefined at x = c without a vertical asymptote. If the multiplicity of c as a real zero of the numerator is at least its multiplicity in the denominator, the output values approach a single value L and the graph has a hole at (c, L).
lesson.context: Topic 1.9 compared multiplicities to find vertical asymptotes. This topic covers the other outcome of that comparison, and it uses a two-sided limit to give the coordinates of the hole.

sections.title: 1.10.A · A hole occurs when the numerator's multiplicity is at least the denominator's.

blocks.text: If the multiplicity of a real zero in the numerator is greater than or equal to its multiplicity in the denominator, then the graph of the rational function has a hole at the corresponding input value. The function is undefined there, but after the common factors are removed, no factor of the denominator is 0 at that input value.

sections.takeaway: Numerator multiplicity ≥ denominator multiplicity gives a hole. Otherwise there is a vertical asymptote.

sections.title: 1.10.A · The hole is at (c, L), where lim x→c r(x) = L.

blocks.text: If the graph of r has a hole at x = c, the location of the hole is found from the output values for input values close to c. If those output values are arbitrarily close to L, the hole is at the point (c, L), and lim x→c r(x) = L. In this case lim x→c⁻ r(x) = lim x→c⁺ r(x) = lim x→c r(x) = L.
Analytically, r(x) = (x − 2)(x + 2)/(x − 2) = x + 2 for x ≠ 2, and x + 2 equals 4 at x = 2. So lim x→2 r(x) = 4 and the hole is at (2, 4).

blocks.title: Write it like the AP Exam
blocks.text: Because x − 2 is a factor of both the numerator and the denominator with equal multiplicity, the graph of r has a hole at x = 2. Since lim x→2 r(x) = 4, the hole is located at (2, 4).

blocks.caption: Graph of r(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2): the line y = x + 2 with a hole at (2, 4)
blocks.alt: A straight line rising through (−2, 0) with an open circle at (2, 4), where the function is undefined.

sections.takeaway: Remove the common factor, then evaluate what remains at c to find L.

sections.title: 1.10.A · One function can have both a hole and a vertical asymptote.

blocks.title: Deciding at each real zero of the denominator
items: Factor the numerator and the denominator completely.
If the zero's multiplicity in the numerator is at least its multiplicity in the denominator, there is a hole. Find L with a limit.
Otherwise there is a vertical asymptote. Describe it with one-sided limits.

blocks.text: For r(x) = (x − 1)(x + 3)/((x − 1)(x − 2)): at x = 1 the multiplicities are equal, so there is a hole, and lim x→1 r(x) = (1 + 3)/(1 − 2) = −4, so the hole is at (1, −4). At x = 2 the numerator is not 0, so there is a vertical asymptote at x = 2.

blocks.caption: Graph of r(x) = (x − 1)(x + 3)/((x − 1)(x − 2)): a hole at (1, −4) and a vertical asymptote at x = 2
blocks.alt: A two-branch rational curve with a dashed vertical asymptote at x = 2, a dashed horizontal asymptote at y = 1, and an open circle at (1, −4) on the left branch.

sections.takeaway: Check every real zero of the denominator separately.

vocabulary.definition: A point (c, L) missing from the graph of a function that is undefined at x = c while lim x→c of the function equals L.
A factor that appears in both the numerator and the denominator of a rational function.

connections.title: Two outcomes of one comparison
connections.body: Topic 1.9 found a vertical asymptote when a zero's multiplicity in the denominator is greater than in the numerator. When it is not greater, the graph has a hole.
connections.transferQuestion: What single comparison decides between a hole and a vertical asymptote at x = c?
connections.feedback: Compare the multiplicity of c as a zero of the numerator with its multiplicity as a zero of the denominator.

connections.title: Factored form reveals holes
connections.body: Topic 1.11 explains why a factored form is the best representation for finding real zeros, holes, asymptotes, domain, and range.
connections.transferQuestion: Why might an expanded form hide a hole?
connections.feedback: The common factor is not visible until the numerator and denominator are factored.

glossary.definition: The number of times a linear factor (x − a) is repeated in a polynomial, which is the multiplicity of the zero a.
Notation such as lim x→∞ p(x) = −∞ that describes what the output values do as the input values increase without bound, decrease without bound, or approach a value.
A function analytically represented as a quotient of two polynomial functions, p(x)/q(x).
A line x = a near which the output values of a function increase or decrease without bound as the input values approach a.
A limit as the input values approach a only from values greater than a, written x→a⁺, or only from values less than a, written x→a⁻.
A point (c, L) missing from the graph of a function that is undefined at x = c while lim x→c of the function equals L.
A factor that appears in both the numerator and the denominator of a rational function.
